content.overview: BNS s. 25 — Act not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done by consent.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Act not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done by consent. BNS restatement of IPC 87. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 87. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 25 is the rule on “Act not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done by consent”. The section provides that nothing which is not intended to cause death, or grievous hurt, and which is not known by the doer to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, to any person, above eighteen years of age, who has given consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm; or by reason of any harm which it may be known by the doer to be likely to cause to any such person who has consented to take the risk of that harm. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 25 exists so that “Act not intended and not known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done by consent” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
25. Nothing which is not intended to cause death, or grievous hurt, and which is not known by the doer to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, to any person, above eighteen years of age, who has given consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm; or by reason of any harm which it may be known by the doer to be likely to cause to any such person who has consented to take the risk of that harm

Essential ingredients
1. Nothing which is not intended to cause death, or grievous hurt, and which is not known by the doer to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, to any person, above eighteen years of age, who has given consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm; or by reason of any harm which it may be known by the doer to be likely to cause to any such person who has consented to take the risk of that harm

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A and Z agree to fence with each other for amusement. This agreement implies the consent of each to suffer any harm which, in the course of such fencing, may be caused without foul play; and if A, while playing fairly, hurts Z, A commits no offence

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 25 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Nothing which is not intended to cause death, or grievous hurt, and which is not known by the doer to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, to any person, above eighteen years of age, who has given consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm; or by reason of any harm which it may be known by the doer to be likely to cause to any such person who has consented to take the risk of that harm
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 25 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 25 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: Understand the doctrine of volenti non fit injuria as codified in BNS s. 25.
Examine the statutory limits: the act must not be intended or known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt.
Analyze the requirement of valid consent (express or implied) by a person above eighteen years of age.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 25 provides that nothing which is not intended to cause death, or grievous hurt, and which is not known by the doer to be likely to cause death, or grievous hurt, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, to any person, above eighteen years of age, who has given consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm; or by reason of any harm which it may be known by the doer to be likely to cause to any such person who has consented to take the risk of that harm.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A person who voluntarily consents to run the risk of ordinary harm in lawful activities (such as sports, games, or social interactions) cannot treat that harm as a criminal offence, provided the actor neither intended nor knew the act was likely to cause death or grievous hurt.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 25 (corresponding to IPC s. 87).
Negative limits on harm: Actor must NOT intend to cause death or grievous hurt, and must NOT know the act is likely to cause death or grievous hurt.
Age of consenting party: The person consenting must be above eighteen years of age.
Nature of consent: Consent may be express (written/spoken) or implied (participation in recognized sports).
Consent validity: Must comply with s. 28 (not obtained under fear, misconception, or unsoundness).
essentialIngredients: The act is done with the consent (express or implied) of the victim to suffer harm or take the risk of harm.
The person giving consent is above eighteen years of age.
The doer does not intend to cause death or grievous hurt.
The doer does not know the act to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 25 codifies the principle of volenti non fit injuria in the context of lawful games, sports, and entertainment. When two adults engage in a lawful game of cricket, football, or boxing under recognized rules, each impliedly consents to suffer the incidental knocks, bruises, or minor harms that routinely occur in that sport. The protection fails if the participant breaches the rules with intent to cause serious injury, or uses an intrinsically lethal weapon. A duel with live blades or firearms cannot be protected by s. 25 because death or grievous hurt is inherently intended or known to be likely, and the law does not permit consent to lethal risks.
examples: Teaching example (Lawful sport): Two adults, A and B, agree to fence with safety-tipped foils and protective equipment according to standard sporting rules. During a bout, B's foil slips and causes a minor puncture to A's arm. Section 25 protects B because there was no intention or knowledge of likelihood of death or grievous hurt.

Teaching example (Deadly duel): Two adults agree to fight with loaded revolvers in a private duel. Even though both consented freely, s. 25 does not apply because death or grievous hurt is known to be likely and intended.
distinctions: Section 25 vs Section 26: Section 25 applies to any lawful activity (including games) without requiring 'benefit' to the person, but bars likelihood of death or grievous hurt. Section 26 applies to acts done for the 'benefit' of the person (e.g. surgical operations) and permits risk of grievous hurt or even likelihood of death, provided death is not intended.
Express vs Implied consent: Express consent is directly stated; implied consent is inferred from voluntary participation in a known activity with customary rules.
Lawful sport vs Unlawful violence: Consent cannot legitimize prize fights or duels that violate public peace or involve lethal hazards.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a football player who broke an opponent's collarbone in a regulation tackle can claim the protection of BNS s. 25.
Rule: Section 25 protects an actor where the consenting party is above 18 and harm caused was not intended or known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt.

Application: Check the victim's age. Examine whether the tackle adhered to the ordinary rules and spirit of the sport, or whether it was a deliberate, foul assault intended to maim. If the tackle was within normal sporting play, the risk was impliedly consented to.
Conclusion: If within recognized sporting bounds and without intent to inflict grievous hurt, s. 25 applies.
